title: Africa’s green mineral future: the real mineral processing challenge
body:
Much of the policy and academic debate assumes that mineral processing is not happening in Africa.

That assumption is not entirely true.

Mineral processing is taking place across the continent as our recent report (https://lnkd.in/eyQZNxwP) clearly shows).

The real challenge is not whether Africa processes minerals, but the scale, scope, and variety of that processing.

Evidence from examining export data is sobering:

- The range of processed mineral exports does not reflect Africa’s vast and diverse mineral endowment
- Processed mineral exports are highly concentrated in a few countries such as the DRC, Morocco, South Africa, and Zambia
- Processing remains technologically shallow, with most products requiring further refining abroad before use in high-tech industries. Hence, much of the economic value is realized outside the continent

To be blunt, Africa’s mineral processing profile is heavily tilted toward raw and semi-processed exports.

- The scope of processing is narrow
- The scale is nowhere near what is needed to drive national, regional, or continental structural transformation
- The variety of processed minerals falls far short of Africa’s resource potential

The uncomfortable truth? Africa’s mineral wealth is not translating into industrial power—not because it fails to process minerals, but because it fails to process them seriously.

- Processing without depth, scale, and technological ambition changes very little. It is just not transformative!
- This also matters for countries that impose export bans on unprocessed minerals. Too often, firms respond by doing the bare minimum processing needed to circumvent regulations—without building meaningful local capabilities.

The takeaway:

- Africa has the resources. Now it must expand capabilities to ensure mineral processing moves beyond isolated pockets and evolves into a continent-wide, technologically sophisticated ecosystem.
- The evidence of mineral processing across the continent challenges the dominant narrative—and convenient excuse—that Africa lacks pre-existing capability. While upskilling and further capability building remain essential, the data clearly shows that Africa is not starting from scratch.
- The problem is not absence. It is insufficient scale, weak depth, and limited strategic intent.

If mineral processing is going to matter, it must stop being symbolic—and start being strategic.

A regionally led strategy, rather than a purely country-by-country approach, offers a more credible pathway forward.

Solomon Owusu Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Woubet Kassa, PhD
